scenes.name: El soul se vuelve funky
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la Bomba de James Brown, el soul dio un giro radical: el acento en el primer tiempo se oyó en «Superstition» de Stevie Wonder, «Inner City Blues» de Marvin Gaye y «Cloud Nine» de los Temptations; lo que empezó como un efecto se volvió norma, y el jam funk pasó a ser imprescindible para que un artista negro llegara a la gente en los setenta. Marvin Gaye preguntó «What’s Goin’ On».

scenes.name: Naked funk: la era Reagan
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La era del naked funk abarca las cimas de Prince, Michael Jackson y los dos mandatos de Reagan: recortes, desindustrialización, millones de sin techo, la «guerra contra las drogas» en lugar de contra la pobreza y, desde 1982, el crack. La música negra se volvió narcisista y escapista, del «yo primero»; las bandas, demasiado caras para la ciudad. La industria ofrecía estereotipos (banda pop, crooner, banda funk guarra, según Jon Pareles), MTV no ponía vídeos negros hasta Thriller y Jackson y Prince marcaron las cuotas del crossover. En 1975 trece números 1 R&B eran funk; en 1985 diecisiete de veinte eran baladas. Warner echó a Clinton y CBS sepultó «Pumpin’ It Up»; murieron o se convirtieron Hathaway, Joe Tex, Marvin Gaye, Al Green, Larry Graham. Las máquinas sustituyeron vientos, órgano (el Yamaha DX7), batería y bajo: solo sobrevivió la guitarra rítmica sobre el bajo sintetizado y la palmada electrónica. La insinuación dejó paso al sexo explícito sin cerebro («Do Me Baby», «Beep a Freak»), y llegaron el bass de Miami (2 Live Crew), Egyptian Lover, el New Jack Swing de Teddy Riley y la farsa de Milli Vanilli. Los funkers de verdad abandonaron la radio: el underground (hip hop, go-go) llevó el funk adelante.

podcast.title: Collaboration with Stevie Wonder
podcast.body: Robert Margouleff and Malcolm Cecil collaborated extensively with Stevie Wonder on three pivotal albums in the 1970s: "Talking Book," "Innervisions," and "Fulfillingness' First Finale." Wonder sought their expertise in synthesizers to realize his musical visions, resulting in some of his most iconic and electronically rich songs. "Malcolm, Cecil and their Tonto setup, worked with Stevie on three albums that make up much of the core of Stevie Wonder's greatest period."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Influence on Quincy Jones and Michael Jackson
podcast.body: Robert Margouleff's work with TONTO, particularly its impact on Stevie Wonder's music, caught the attention of Quincy Jones. The knowledge and techniques gained from TONTO influenced Jones's production of Michael Jackson's albums, ushering in new possibilities for electronically generated music in mainstream pop. "Quincy Jones loved this thing. What he learned shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums and it brought all kinds of new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

podcast.title: Pioneering Electronic Music with TONTO
podcast.body: In the late 1960s, American record producer Robert Margouleff, alongside British jazz musician Malcolm Cecil, was captivated by Bob Moog's new synthesizers. They embarked on creating TONTO (The Original New Timbral Orchestra), the world's largest modular synth setup. This colossal instrument, built with components from various manufacturers, enabled unprecedented sonic textures and multi-layered compositions, significantly impacting electronic music production. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."

xref.title: Break from Motown and Synth Exploration
xref.body: After leaving his old contract with Motown Records, Stevie Wonder sought out Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff and their TONTO synthesizer for a tutorial. He desired to explore synthesizers to finally record the music he envisioned, marking a significant shift in his artistic direction. "Stevie was out of his old contract with Motown Records and wanted a tutorial and synthesizers so he could finally start recording the music that he heard in his head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

xref.title: Career Transformation with TONTO
xref.body: Stevie Wonder's collaboration with Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff, utilizing the TONTO synthesizer, profoundly changed the direction of his career. This partnership led to his "greatest period" in the 1970s, encompassing iconic albums like "Talking Book," "Innervisions," and "Fulfillingness' First Finale," and fundamentally altered the landscape of Black Pop music. "Tonto changed the direction of Stevie Wonder's career. And he changed what Black Pop music could be."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

xref.title: Collaboration with Stevie Wonder
xref.body: Stevie Wonder, after hearing TONTO, contacted Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff, seeking a tutorial in synthesizers as he was free from his Motown contract and wanted to record the music in his head. Cecil and Margouleff worked with Wonder on three albums — "Talking Book," "Innervisions," and "Fulfillingness' First Finale" — over three and a half years in the 1970s, which constitute a core period of Wonder's career. Songs like "Superstition," "Living for the City," "Boogie On Reggae Woman," and "Higher Ground" were all composed and recorded using TONTO. "Stevie Wonder heard Tonto and called up Malcolm and Cecil. Stevie was out of his old contract with Motown Records and wanted a tutorial and synthesizers so he could finally start recording the music that he heard in his head."

xref.title: Influence from TONTO on Production
xref.body: Quincy Jones was greatly impressed by the TONTO synthesizer and its capabilities. What he learned from Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff's work with the instrument significantly influenced how he produced Michael Jackson's albums, thereby bringing new attention to the potential of electronically generated music. "Quincy Jones loved this thing. What he learned shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums and it brought all kinds of new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music."

xref.title: Influence on Black Pop and Quincy Jones
xref.body: Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff's work with TONTO, particularly on Stevie Wonder's albums, changed the direction of Wonder's career and redefined what Black Pop music could be. Quincy Jones was highly impressed by TONTO, and what he learned from it shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums, drawing new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music. "Tonto changed the direction of Stevie Wonder's career. And he changed what Black Pop music could be. Quincy Jones loved this thing. What he learned shaped how he produced Michael Jackson's albums and it brought all kinds of new attention to the possibilities of electronically generated music."

xref.title: Inventor of the Synthesizer
xref.body: Bob Moog is recognized as the inventor of the synthesizer. His new machines captivated Malcolm Cecil and Robert Margouleff in the late 1960s, inspiring them to build TONTO, the massive modular synth that profoundly influenced electronic music. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Unsung Heroes of Music: Part 1

xref.title: Pioneering Electronic Music with TONTO
xref.body: In the late 1960s, Malcolm Cecil, a British jazz musician working for the BBC, along with American record producer Robert Margouleff, were fascinated by new synthesizers from Bob Moog. They set out to construct the world's largest modular synth setup, which they named TONTO (The Original New Timbral Orchestra). This behemoth, comprising gear from Moog, Oberheim, ARP, EMS, Roland, and Yamaha, allowed for unprecedented sound creation and multi-track performance, profoundly influencing electronic music. "These guys, a British jazz dude working for the BBC and an American record producer, were huge influences on the world of electronic music, but they were almost entirely behind the scenes."
